summary:
İzmir stands under the national framework of Turkey. Turkey has no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers, so the visitor-facing exposure lies inside the country. Foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance. That general requirement intersects with identity checks aimed at trans people on the street: bianet reports that on 31 July 2025 trans women in a large-city entertainment district were subjected to mass identity-document roundups, with names recorded and videos taken and no official reason given. In August 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in Beyoğlu, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released them after 'General Information Gathering' background checks; legal experts quoted by bianet argue those checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Nothing was fined in that episode, but names and details were recorded.

Criminalisation by statute had not been enacted when Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025, but a leaked draft of Türkiye's omnibus 11th Judicial Package then before the government would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality and its promotion with up to three years' prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. The draft would amend civil code article 40 to raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing deemed-illegal interventions would face fines and up to seven years' prison, trans people receiving such care up to three years, with courts able to order pretrial detention. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warns it would force treatment into unregulated underground settings. Whether the package has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

Kaos GL's report 'A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy' finds that hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy. It records 313 violations of the right to liberty in 2025, roughly two and a half times the previous year, citing detentions, arrests and criminal cases against Pride participants as the main reasons, alongside 89 torture or ill-treatment violations and six right-to-life violations, three of them recorded as hate-motivated killings with trans people the most affected. For the first time in many years an LGBTI+ association was closed and criminal cases were opened against 11 of its members for human rights advocacy.

Policing asymmetry is documented at the level of individual cases. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a state hate policy. On 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; an opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Trans visitors who are detained are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare. Some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other male inmates. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Protection machinery is thin. Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct discrimination protection for gender identity. The European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis, while noting official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion. If medication is needed during a stay, hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.
tangentialFactors:
The draft 11th Judicial Package sits within a broader authoritarian drift, and the Erdoğan government has repeatedly used 'the family' and 'public morals' framing to legitimise stigmatisation of LGBT people. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association publicly opposed the draft, indicating organised domestic resistance to the legislative direction rather than passive acceptance.

İzmir is one province within a national pattern in which the documented violations are concentrated in Istanbul, Ankara and other large cities. The 313 recorded violations of 2025 are national figures compiled by Kaos GL, and the closure of an LGBTI+ association with criminal cases against 11 members marks a first in many years, signalling that participation in advocacy carries legal risk country-wide.

The ID-carrying regime with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira applies to all foreigners at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations; for trans visitors it compounds a documented pattern of street-level identity checks in which names and photographs are taken without stated legal basis. Legal experts quoted by bianet argue that the resulting 'General Information Gathering' checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Discriminatory rhetoric by senior officials is identified in monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week as a driver of deepening homophobia and transphobia, and the European Commission's 2025 report notes official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion. Public events therefore remain sites of exposure rather than protected assembly.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted since Human Rights Watch's 29 October 2025 report is unresolved in the sources. The draft's provisions as described are drawn from a leaked text and had not been adopted at the time of reporting.

The official grounds for the 31 July 2025 mass identity-document roundups of trans women were not given, according to bianet, and whether any charges or administrative penalties followed is not sourced. The legal basis asserted by police for the August 2025 'General Information Gathering' checks is disputed by legal experts quoted by bianet but has not been resolved in the available material.

İzmir-specific enforcement data — local detention figures, provincial police practice, or the handling of identity checks in the city — is not present in the source inventory, and the dossier's on-the-ground picture for İzmir rests on national and Istanbul-based documentation. Whether Izmir's own Pride or community facilities face restrictions is not sourced here.

The outcome of the criminal cases against the 11 members of the closed LGBTI+ association, and the findings of any investigation into Poyraz's death, are not stated in the sources.
